title: What are the phases of the Maven build lifecycle (`validate` → `compile` → `test` → `package` → `verify` → `install` → `deploy`), what is the difference between `mvn install` (installs the artifact into the local `.m2` repository) and `mvn deploy` (uploads it to a remote/shared repository), and what is the role of `<distributionManagement>` (configuring the remote artifact repository — e.g. Nexus/Artifactory — that `deploy` publishes to)?
shortTitle: Maven lifecycle phases, `mvn install` vs `mvn deploy`, and `distributionManagement`
topicTitle: What are the phases of the Maven build lifecycle (`validate` → `compile` → `test

s1_definition.profdef: The Maven default build lifecycle is an ordered sequence of phases — validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy — and running any phase executes every phase before it. `mvn install` builds the artifact and places it into your machine's local repository at the dot-m2 folder so other local projects can use it. `mvn deploy` does everything install does and then uploads the artifact to a shared remote repository so other people and CI machines can use it. The `distributionManagement` section in the POM configures the address and credentials of that remote repository, typically Nexus or Artifactory, which the deploy phase publishes to.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of baking a cake for National Bank of India's branches. The lifecycle is the fixed recipe: check ingredients (validate), mix (compile), taste-test (test), box it (package), final quality check (verify), then distribute. `mvn install` is putting the finished cake in your own kitchen fridge so only you and your housemates can eat it — local, private. `mvn deploy` is sending the cake to the central bakery warehouse so every branch in the country can collect it — shared, public to the org. The distributionManagement section is the warehouse's address and your delivery pass, telling deploy exactly where to drop the cake and proving you are allowed to.
s1_definition.oneliner: The lifecycle runs validate through deploy in order; install publishes to your local dot-m2, deploy publishes to the shared remote repo configured by distributionManagement.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Maven default build lifecycle is an ordered sequence of phases — validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy — and running any phase executes every phase before it. `mvn install` builds the artifact and places it into your machine's local repository at the dot-m2 folder so other local projects can use it. `mvn deploy` does everything install does and then uploads the artifact to a shared remote repository so other people and CI machines can use it. The `distributionManagement` section in the POM configures the address and credentials of that remote repository, typically Nexus or Artifactory, which the deploy phase publishes to.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of baking a cake for National Bank of India's branches. The lifecycle is the fixed recipe: check ingredients (validate), mix (compile), taste-test (test), box it (package), final quality check (verify), then distribute. `mvn install` is putting the finished cake in your own kitchen fridge so only you and your housemates can eat it — local, private. `mvn deploy` is sending the cake to the central bakery warehouse so every branch in the country can collect it — shared, public to the org. The distributionManagement section is the warehouse's address and your delivery pass, telling deploy exactly where to drop the cake and proving you are allowed to.

**One line to remember:** The lifecycle runs validate through deploy in order; install publishes to your local dot-m2, deploy publishes to the shared remote repo configured by distributionManagement.

sections.s2_technical:
The Maven default lifecycle is a fixed, ordered chain of phases, and the golden rule is that invoking a phase runs that phase and all phases before it. Let me walk through the main ones. Validate checks that the project is correct and all necessary information is available — the POM is well-formed and required properties exist. Compile compiles the main source code in src/main/java into target/classes. Test runs the unit tests against the compiled code using a testing framework; if tests fail, the build stops here by default, which is exactly what you want so broken code never gets packaged.

Package takes the compiled code and bundles it into its distributable format, usually a jar or war, placed in target. Verify runs any checks on the results of integration tests to ensure quality criteria are met — this is where coverage gates or integration-test plugins commonly bind. Install takes the packaged artifact and copies it into your local repository at the dot-m2 folder on your own machine. Deploy, the final phase, copies the final artifact to a remote shared repository for sharing with other developers and projects. Because of the ordering rule, running mvn deploy silently runs validate, compile, test, package, verify, and install first.

The difference between install and deploy is about scope and audience. mvn install is local and private. It puts the artifact into your machine's dot-m2 repository, so only projects built on that same machine can resolve it as a dependency. This is perfect during local development when, say, you build a shared banking-common library and immediately want your loan-service on the same laptop to pick up the new version. Nobody else and no CI server can see it.

mvn deploy is remote and shared. After doing everything install does, it uploads the artifact to a remote repository manager such as Nexus or Artifactory. Now every developer in the organization and every CI pipeline can declare a dependency on that exact version and download it. This is how versioned, released libraries are shared across teams. In a disciplined setup, developers rarely run deploy from their laptops; instead the CI server runs mvn deploy after tests pass on the main branch, so only reviewed, tested artifacts reach the shared repository.

The distributionManagement section is what makes deploy know where to go. In the POM you add a distributionManagement block with a repository element for release versions and a snapshotRepository element for snapshot versions, each with an id and a url pointing at your Nexus or Artifactory. The id links to credentials stored in your settings.xml, never hardcoded in the POM. Maven distinguishes releases from snapshots: a version ending in -SNAPSHOT, like 1.1.0-SNAPSHOT, is a work-in-progress that can be re-published repeatedly and goes to the snapshotRepository, while a plain version like 1.0.0 is an immutable release that goes to the release repository and should never change once published. A senior-level nuance I always mention: treating released versions as immutable is critical for a bank, because if version 1.0.0 of a payments library could be silently overwritten, a security audit could never trust that the artifact running in production matches what was reviewed. Snapshot versus release separation and an authenticated remote repository give you that traceability and governance.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has a shared library, banking-common, that holds money utilities and the Account model used by every microservice. The team needs a disciplined way to build, locally test, and then publish this library.

Problem 1 — a developer fixes a rounding bug in the money utility and wants the loan-service on the same laptop to immediately use the fixed version before anyone else sees it. This is exactly what mvn install is for — it drops the new jar into the local dot-m2 so local projects pick it up, privately.

Problem 2 — once the fix is reviewed and merged, every team across the bank must get the new version. This is exactly what mvn deploy is for — it uploads the artifact to the shared Nexus so all services and CI pipelines can resolve it.

Problem 3 — an auditor asks for proof that payments-common 1.0.0 in production is byte-identical to what was reviewed. This is exactly why release versions must be immutable and separated from snapshots in distributionManagement — a released version can never be overwritten.

The mini-project is the banking-common library with a MoneyUtil class, a POM that declares distributionManagement for release and snapshot repositories, and the settings.xml credentials reference. We then show the exact commands for install versus deploy and what each produces.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
banking-common/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    ├── main/java/com/bank/common/
    │   └── MoneyUtil.java
    └── test/java/com/bank/common/
        └── MoneyUtilTest.java

~/.m2/settings.xml            (holds Nexus credentials, NOT in the project)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Run just up to 'test' — compiles and tests, nothing packaged yet.
mvn test

# Run the lifecycle up to 'package' — produces target/banking-common-1.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
mvn package

# INSTALL: local only. Copies the jar into THIS machine's ~/.m2 repository.
# Now loan-service on the SAME laptop can depend on 1.1.0-SNAPSHOT.
mvn install
ls ~/.m2/repository/com/bank/banking-common/1.1.0-SNAPSHOT/

# DEPLOY: shared. Does everything install does, THEN uploads to Nexus.
# Because the version ends in -SNAPSHOT, it goes to the snapshotRepository.
mvn deploy

# For a real release: set version to 1.1.0 (no -SNAPSHOT), then deploy.
# It goes to the RELEASE repo and can NEVER be overwritten.
mvn versions:set -DnewVersion=1.1.0
mvn deploy
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a developer fixes MoneyUtil, builds banking-common at version 1.1.0-SNAPSHOT, installs it locally, then CI later deploys it, and finally a release 1.1.0 is published.

Step 1: The developer runs mvn install. Because install is late in the lifecycle, Maven first runs validate, then compile building MoneyUtil into target/classes, then test running the two JUnit tests. Both tests pass, so the build continues.

Step 2: The package phase bundles the compiled class into target/banking-common-1.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar. The install phase then copies that jar into the local repository at dot-m2/repository/com/bank/banking-common/1.1.0-SNAPSHOT.

Step 3: On the same laptop, the loan-service declares a dependency on com.bank:banking-common:1.1.0-SNAPSHOT. When the developer builds loan-service, Maven finds the freshly installed jar in dot-m2 and uses it. Nobody else can see this version yet — it is private to this machine.

Step 4: The fix is reviewed and merged. The CI pipeline runs mvn deploy on the main branch. Deploy repeats the whole lifecycle — validate through install — and then reads distributionManagement. Because the version ends in -SNAPSHOT, Maven uploads the jar to the snapshotRepository URL, authenticating with the nbi-snapshots credentials from settings.xml.

Step 5: Now every developer and every CI pipeline across the bank can resolve 1.1.0-SNAPSHOT from Nexus. Snapshots can be re-published, so a later build of the same snapshot overwrites the previous one, which is fine for work in progress.

Step 6: To cut a formal release, the version is set to 1.1.0 with no -SNAPSHOT and deployed. Maven routes it to the release repository, where it is immutable — attempting to deploy 1.1.0 again is rejected, giving auditors a guarantee that the released artifact never changes.

```
Oct 25, 2026 01:05:02 AM INFO: [maven] install: validate->compile->test(2 passed)->package
Oct 25, 2026 01:05:06 AM INFO: [maven] installed to ~/.m2/.../1.1.0-SNAPSHOT/banking-common-1.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
Oct 25, 2026 01:20:10 AM INFO: [ci] deploy: version ends in -SNAPSHOT -> nbi-snapshots repo
Oct 25, 2026 01:20:14 AM INFO: [ci] uploaded to https://nexus.nbi.internal/.../maven-snapshots/
Oct 25, 2026 02:00:03 AM INFO: [ci] release 1.1.0 -> nbi-releases repo (immutable)
Oct 25, 2026 02:00:05 AM INFO: [ci] re-deploy of 1.1.0 would be REJECTED (immutable)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Lifecycle Phases + install/deploy + distributionManagement ═══

  ┌─ Default Lifecycle (invoking a phase runs ALL earlier ones) ──┐
  │  validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy│
  │  validate : POM well-formed, info present                     │
  │  compile  : src/main/java → target/classes                    │
  │  test     : unit tests; FAIL stops the build                  │
  │  package  : bundle jar/war into target                        │
  │  verify   : integration checks / coverage gates               │
  │  install  : copy artifact → LOCAL ~/.m2                        │
  │  deploy   : upload artifact → REMOTE shared repo              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ install vs deploy ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  install : audience = THIS machine (private, local dev)       │
  │  deploy  : audience = WHOLE org (shared, via Nexus)           │
  │  deploy = install + upload-to-remote                          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── distributionManagement Relationship ────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐   referenced by id   ┌──────────────────┐
  │ pom.xml                  │─────────────────────▶│ settings.xml     │
  │ <distributionManagement> │   (credentials)       │ <server id=      │
  │  <repository> releases   │                       │  "nbi-releases"> │
  │  <snapshotRepository>    │                       │ user/token       │
  └────────────┬─────────────┘                       └──────────────────┘
               │ mvn deploy routes by version type
               ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ -SNAPSHOT → snapshot repo │  (re-publishable)
  │ plain x.y.z → release repo│  (IMMUTABLE)
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Artifact Lifecycle ─────────────────────

  [compiled] ──package──→ [jar in target] ──install──→ [in ~/.m2 LOCAL]
                                 │
                                 │ deploy
                                 ▼
                     ┌───────────────────────────┐
                     │ -SNAPSHOT → SNAPSHOT repo  │──re-deploy──▶ [overwritten OK]
                     │ release   → RELEASE repo   │──re-deploy──▶ [REJECTED immutable]
                     └───────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (mvn deploy) ────────────────────────────────

  1. mvn deploy
  2.   → validate → compile → test → package → verify → install
  3.   → read <distributionManagement>
  4.   → detect version type (SNAPSHOT vs release)
  5.   → look up credentials by <id> in settings.xml
  6.   → upload artifact + POM + checksums to Nexus
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Maven default build lifecycle is a fixed, ordered sequence of phases — validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy — and the key rule is that invoking any phase runs that phase and every phase before it. Validate checks the project is correct, compile builds the main sources, test runs the unit tests and stops the build if they fail so broken code is never packaged, package bundles the jar or war, verify runs integration and quality checks, install places the artifact locally, and deploy publishes it remotely. So when I run deploy, Maven quietly runs everything from validate through install first.

The difference between install and deploy is scope and audience. mvn install is local and private — it copies the built artifact into my own machine's dot-m2 repository, so only projects on that same machine can resolve it. That is exactly what I want during local development when I fix a shared library and immediately want another service on the same laptop to pick up the change. mvn deploy is remote and shared — it does everything install does and then uploads the artifact to a shared repository manager like Nexus or Artifactory, so every developer and every CI pipeline in the organization can depend on that exact version.

The distributionManagement section in the POM is what tells deploy where to publish. It defines a release repository and a snapshot repository, each with an id and a URL, and the id links to credentials stored safely in settings.xml rather than in the POM. Maven distinguishes a snapshot version, which ends in dash SNAPSHOT and can be re-published repeatedly for work in progress, from a plain release version, which is immutable once published.

At National Bank of India I used exactly this flow for a shared banking-common library. During development I ran install so my loan-service on the same laptop picked up a rounding fix privately. After review, the CI pipeline ran deploy so the whole bank could use the new snapshot, and formal versions were released as immutable artifacts. I always stress the immutability of releases, because for a bank it is a governance and audit requirement — if a released payments library could be silently overwritten, a security audit could never trust that what runs in production matches what was reviewed. Separating snapshots from releases and publishing through an authenticated remote repository gives you that traceability.
